properties.comments: Verified emergency management and public confirmed tornado damage via video. Broader survey not conducted due to no other damage reports. Minor damage to home, multiple trees uprooted, shed/garage doors blown in and uplifted. Damage consistent with EF-0 indicators.

This tornado began near the intersection of Phillips Avenue and Ramsey Blvd. on the southwest end of Keyes. Here it snapped a few branches off of some elm trees and did damage to an older mobile home by pushing it a few feet, despite being anchored down. The tornado then continued northeast where it lifted an empty grain silo and either rolled or tossed or a combination of both across a field and landed about 100 yards or so to the northeast. It also snapped the top of a power pole. The tornado continued northeast  It caused some minor roof damage to the community center, including the collapse of one of the walls and destroyed the sidewalk awning connecting the two buildings. Another power pole was also broken in a couple of spots. This location likely had an enhancement of wind due to the enclosed nature of the area. The tornado crossed Jefferson Avenue and caused some damage to a carport awning and snapped tree branches and a softwood tree. The most damage was around Polk Street where it resulted in the collapse of an old pool hall, lifted the roof off a building across the street, which resulted in the collapse of an exterior wall. It then produced additional damage to a large barn like structure along Monroe Avenue. It was after this point that the tornado likely lifted as little in the way of damage was noted. Much of the damage along the path was done to older, less well built structures and this contributed to a lower rating. It also created a very narrow path through town from southwest to northeast.

A tornado developed south of I-25 with more impactful damage starting in the Via Caballero neighborhood in the south central portion of Santa Fe just north of I-25. The tornado traveled northward for approximately 2.25 miles, terminating near the College of Santa Fe. Much of the damage was along Rancho Siringo and Camino Chueco Roads. Damage included broken power poles, uprooted or damaged trees, damage to roofs. Ten homes sustained damaged with one home having the majority of the roof removed and a collapsed wall. This tornado has been given a rating of EF-1 with peak winds of 110 mph.
A very brief tornado moved across a farmstead approximately 5 miles northeast of Madison, resulting in a broken tree and other minor tree damage.

NWS Storm Survey found damage consistent with a brief tornado west of Clark in rural southern Randolph County around 10:42 am on Tuesday, November 3rd.  The tornado began near the intersection of Route B and County Road 2690, moving to the north northeast where it damaged a farmstead along 2690, inflicting damage to trees and farm outbuildings. The tornado ended near the intersection of County Roads 2690 and D234. The max estimated wind speeds were around 90 mph. The tornado traveled around 1 mile in length, was 50 yards in width, and was on the ground for around 2 minutes.

This weak tornado, originating from a quasi-linear convective system, began just south of Holmes Road in far northwestern DeSoto Parish in a rural and wooded area. It then continued northeastward in a predominantly rural area, crossing into far southwestern Caddo Parish and ending just west of Four Forks Road and south of the Four Forks community.  Despite the radar showing a few tornadic debris signatures, the damage was confined to relatively light tree damage with no tree snaps or uproots. This limited the survey team's rating to an EF-0.

This same thunderstorm line segment advanced northeast, prompting a few tornado warnings in Shreveport and Bossier City. A tornadic debris signature was noted near Bert Kouns Road, approximately 3 miles south-southeast of the Shreveport Airport.  However, the NWS survey team could not find ratable damage there. The team theorizes that a sub-tornadic mesovortex with peak winds less than 65 mph in this area still managed to loft enough leaves and pine needles to generate the brief and shallow tornadic debris signal on the close by WSR-88D. There was a lot of this vegetative leaf litter observed in this area. The survey team has noted this occurring a few times previously during this time of year due to leaves beginning to shed. Of course, the ongoing drought stressing trees probably additionally contributed to easy shedding of leaves and pine needles.

Around 10:17am on November 3rd, 2026, a mini supercell developed out ahead of a quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) near the Texas and Louisiana border to the west of Mooringsport, LA. This mini supercell produced a very brief EF-0 tornado that touched down on Parish Road 136 between the Black Bayou and Highway 49. The tornado downed a large hardwood tree along this Parish Road as it then continued northeast towards Highway 49. Before the tornado reached Highway 49, it moved across the intersection of Parish Road 136 and Gamm Road, where a storm spotter captured a geotagged photo of the tornado lifting just west of Highway 49.  The storm survey team consulted numerous residents, law enforcement officials, and utility workers to help determine whether the tornado track continued beyond Highway 49 after witnessing a lack of additional damage, and these conversations led the team to conclude that there was no additional damage from this storm. The team did investigate the area around what was determined to a be a tornado debris signature (TDS) on radar to the southwest of Highway 49 and HWY 530/Belcher Oil City Road, but did not find any damage indicators. The team has theorized that the TDS could have been the result of a sub-tornadic mesovortex which may have lofted enough leaves and/or pine needles in this particular area for the WSR-88D to detect. ..

This tornado developed south of Big Sky Lane and east of the S 4060 Road. It moved northeast, crossing Big Sky Lane and the E 360 Road, snapping numerous large tree limbs before moving into open terrain. The tornado dissipated south of the E 340 Road. It produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D radar, and was likely more intense north of the E 360 Road (based on radar data), but any damage in that part of the path was inaccessible by road, and therefore, couldn't be assessed.

This tornado developed south of the E 390 Road and east of the N 435 Road. It moved north-northeast across the E 390 Road, where numerous trees were uprooted, and a home and outbuilding were damaged. The tornado then moved through open terrain that was inaccessible by road for about a mile and a half. It then snapped several power poles south of the E 370 Road, uprooted trees along the E 370 Road and S 4360 Road, and dissipated south of the E 360 Road. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

This tornado developed over rugged terrain west of Cedarville on a ridgetop. It moved north-northeast across Rocky Road and Shiloh Road, where trees were uprooted and a few were snapped, and numerous large tree limbs were snapped. The tornado then moved northeast through rugged terrain after crossing Broken Trail, and then uprooted a few trees and snapped large tree limbs along Creekside Way and finally on Highway 59 before dissipating. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KSRX WSR-88D.

Chaser video showed the circulation was on the ground west of Singhurst Street before it crossed the street and partially destroyed a barn and pushed an RV off its foundation. The tornado then continued through tree groves but caused no additional damage. Chaser footage showed the circulation was still in contact with the ground as far east as State Road 159.
